stages.why: How long a part takes to go from an idea to a box in the garage (plan 5.1). At full capacity the four stages run 10, 28, 32 and 24 days: about three months, so a season fits four or five upgrades on one part and a team must choose where they go. Research and design are the stages the wind tunnel actually shortens — 60% and 40% of the work there is aero time, the rest is people — while a concept is a drawing and production is a shop floor, and neither goes faster for a bigger tunnel.

capacity.why: What the design office gets through (plan 5.6: an overloaded department works slower and worse). A department of 80 people at quality 60 is the reference and does a stage in the days above; quality counts for 60% of the difference and headcount for 40%, so a small sharp office beats a big blunt one but not by everything. Three projects at once are free; every project over that costs 22% of the office's speed, down to a quarter — a team that runs eight projects finishes none of them on time, which is exactly the trap the plan wants available.

gain.why: What an upgrade is worth in points of a part's rating (plan 5.1). A team with aerodynamics at 60 and a normal share of the tunnel finds about 3.2 points — a tenth of a second or so once it reaches the car — and each point of department quality adds 0.035, so a top aero group finds 4.6 where a weak one finds 1.8. Giving a project the whole tunnel adds up to 1.6 points on top: the allowance is the real currency of the season. Nothing ever returns less than 0.4 points, because a team that spends three months on a part does learn something. Money follows the same shape: 1.4M a stage plus up to 2.2M for the tunnel time, so a four-stage upgrade with half the tunnel costs about 6.7M of the cap.

uncertainty.why: How well a team knows what it has built before it runs it (plan 5.1: the interval is the mechanic, and it narrows with the aerodynamicists, the simulator and the tunnel time spent). At the concept the expected gain is worth ±1.1 points at aero 60 — a third of the gain itself, so signing a project off is genuinely a bet; research cuts that to 65% and design to 40%, which is when a part stops being an argument and starts being a plan. The three sources of precision together are worth about a third of the width, not all of it: each point of aero quality takes off 0.004, each simulator level 0.05, full tunnel time 0.2, so even the best factory signs off a concept it is not sure about. Nothing goes under 0.25 points before the part runs: the tunnel is not the track, which is what the correlation below is about.

correlation.why: The gap between the tunnel and the track (plan 5.1, 5.17). A team's hidden correlation bias — realised gain over predicted, minus one, drawn at world creation in the pack's own -0.5..0.5 range — multiplies every upgrade it builds: a factory at -0.2 quietly gets a fifth less than it measured, an honest one gets what it measured. On top of that every part has its own 0.35-point surprise, so one good upgrade proves nothing. The team never sees the bias: it sees the part on track, measured to 0.25 points, and works the bias out over several upgrades from a prior 0.15 wide — which is why plan 5.17 makes the preseason test the moment of truth.

philosophy.why: The season's direction (plan 5.1). A project that fits the philosophy finds 20% more; one that pulls the other way 12% less. Changing philosophy mid-season writes off 35% of the progress of everything not yet built: the cost is real but survivable, so it is a decision and not a trap.

freshness.why: What a part costs before it has any miles on it (plan 5.1: an upgrade is a risk as well as a gain). A brand-new part takes 6 percentage points off the car's reliability — with a car around 0.93 that roughly doubles the chance of a failure on the weekend it first runs, which is exactly the choice the plan wants: fit it now and race it green, or run the known part one more round. It beds in over four weeks, so a part fitted two races ago is as safe as anything else on the car.
